title: Technical Appendix
text:
This project analyzes Billboard Hot 100 chart data from January 2016 through December 2025. The pipeline consists of three stages: scraping raw chart data, cleaning and normalizing artist names, and then wrangling the data and computing metrics and statistics for visualization.
All code is written in Python. Visualizations are produced using Matplotlib, Seaborn, Plotly, and Altair and embedded in a Quarto website using the Closeread extension for scrollytelling.
Link to GitHub Repo: https://github.com/rvt9bx/dsan5200-project.



Chart data was collected using the billboard.py Python package, which scrapes the Billboard website for historical chart data.
Script: billboard_scrape.py
The scraper iterates over every Saturday from January 2, 2016 to December 27, 2025 since Billboard publishes new charts on a weekly Saturday schedule. For each date, it fetches the full Hot 100 chart and writes one row per song entry to a CSV file.
Each row contains the following fields:



Field
Description




chart_date
Date of the chart (Saturday)


rank
Chart position (1–100)


title
Song title


artist
Artist credit as listed by Billboard


weeks_on_chart
Cumulative weeks on chart at time of entry


peak_position
Highest chart position the song has reached


last_position
Chart position the previous week


is_new
Whether this is the song’s chart debut



Individual failed requests (network errors, rate limiting) are logged and skipped without interrupting the full run. The output is written to data/hot100_history.csv.



Notebook: data_cleaning.ipynb
The raw CSV required three cleaning steps before analysis: HTML tag removal, artist name splitting, and date parsing.


Some artist name fields returned by the Billboard scraper contain HTML anchor tags. These were stripped using a regex that removes any content between < and >.



Billboard credits collaborative songs with compound artist strings, such as "Taylor Swift Featuring Ed Sheeran" or "Bad Bunny & Jhayco". To count a song toward each credited artist, these strings are split into a list of individual names.
Splitting is complicated by band names that contain separator words. For example, "Tones And I" should not be split on "And". A blocklist of known band names is protected before splitting by replacing them with placeholder tokens, then restoring them after. The resulting artist_list column contains a Python list of individual artist names per row. When computing per-artist statistics and creating visualizations, the dataframe is exploded on this column so that each artist in a collaboration gets their own row.



The cleaned dataframe is saved to data/clean_hot100_history.csv with the original columns plus year and artist_list.




Part of Notebook: viz.ipynb


Some songs have gaps in their chart history, where they fell off the Hot 100 and then re-entered. For visualizations that show a song’s full timeline (such as the heatmap and timeline strip), these gaps need to be represented explicitly as missing weeks rather than simply absent rows, so that the time axis renders correctly.
For each song, a complete weekly date range is generated between its first and last chart appearance using pd.date_range with a Saturday frequency to match Billboard’s publication schedule. This full range is then left-merged with the song’s actual chart data, producing null rank values for any weeks the song was not on the chart. Songs with no gaps are returned unchanged.
The result is saved to data/filled_hot100_history.csv, where every song has one row per Saturday between its debut and final chart appearance, with rank = NaN for weeks it was absent. This allows visualizations to correctly render gaps as blank space rather than connecting non-consecutive weeks with a continuous line or bar.




Part of Notebook: viz.ipynb
Two key metrics were computed per song to categorize chart behavior: rise rate and decay rate. Both are defined as the slope of rank change over time, measured in chart positions per week.


Rise rate measures how quickly a song climbed to its peak. It is defined as the average positions gained per week between a song’s debut and its peak week:
\[\text{rise rate} = \frac{\text{debut rank} - \text{peak rank}}{\text{weeks to peak}}\]
A higher rise rate means a faster climb. Songs that debut at their peak rank (i.e., peak week = 0) are assigned a rise rate of 0. Songs that only chart for one week are excluded.
Because Billboard rank numbers are inverted (rank 1 is the best), subtracting peak rank from debut rank gives a positive number when the song climbed.
The resulting dataframe of one row per unique artist–song pair is saved at data/rise_rates.csv. It includes general song identifiers as well as columns total_weeks, peak_rank, debut_rank, peak_week, and rise_rate.



Decay rate measures how quickly a song fell after reaching its peak. It is defined as the slope between peak rank and end rank over the number of post-peak weeks:
\[\text{decay rate} = -\frac{\text{end rank} - \text{peak rank}}{\text{post-peak weeks}}\]
The negation means a song that falls down the chart (increasing rank number) gets a negative decay rate. A decay rate close to 0 means a song held its position; a large negative value means a sharp drop. Songs that end the chart run at their peak (no post-peak data) are assigned a decay rate of 0. Songs that only chart for one week are excluded.
The resulting dataframe of one row per unique artist–song pair is saved at data/decay_rates.csv. It includes general song identifiers as well as columns total_weeks, peak_rank, debut_rank, end_rank, peak_week, decay_rate, and post_peak_length.




Part of Notebook: viz.ipynb
Aside from the Altair linked view, which is generated directly within index.qmd, all code for the visualizations and summary statistics in this project are included in viz.ipynb.

title: Flashor Burn
text:
Billboard Hot 100 · 2016–2025
  
  Can we measure the virality or endurability of songs with the Billboard Hot 100 Charts? Dive in to explore different artists and the music landscape of the past decade.
  Eleanor Byrd   ·  Spring 2026
All Sources
AI Usage Log
Technical Appendix

title: Flashor Burn
text:
What is the Billboard Hot 100?
For some background, the Billboard Hot 100 is a music popularity ranking that originated in its current form in 1958 3. Published weekly, it is a list of the most popular singles, originally based on radio airplay and the sales of the song, but now incorporates streaming data as well 4. If you hear that a song is “Number 1,” that means that it has reached the peak ranking of #1 on the Billboard Hot 100. This article examines the Billboard Hot 100 data from January 2016 to December 2025, for a total of 522 weeks, 5869 songs, and 1472 artists, scraped using billboard.py 5.

title: Flashor Burn
section: How do we capture a flash or a burn?
text:
How do we capture a flash or a burn?
In order to quantify a song’s climb up the chart and its fall down it, we calculate rise and decay rates. Both of these metrics are constructed as the change in ranks per week, where rise rate is positive and calcluated based on the data from a song’s debut to its peak, and the decay rate is negative and is calculated from a song’s peak to its last day on the chart. Put simply, they are slopes: the rise rate is the average number of ranks a song increases per week up until its peak, and the decay rate is the average number of ranks a song decreases per week after peaking. A rise rate of 0 means that a song debuts at its peak, and a decay rate of 0 means it ends at its peak.
While these metrics provide a general assessment, they do have limitations. They only incorporate the initial ranking of a song, the peak ranking, the end ranking, and the number of weeks in between those points. Thus the rise and decay rates do not take into account the variability in a song’s ranking before or after it reaches its peak. More influential for the decay rate calculations, songs that drop of the chart completely and then re-enter have extended post-peak lengths, and the final rank it ends on could be much higher than a lower rank it previously disappeared from. Thus the decay rate can appear very slow for a song that could have several flashes of popularity on the charts.

title: Flashor Burn
section: How did virality change over time?
text:
How did virality change over time?
Now that you’ve seen some specific examples, let’s dive into how these measures of popularity rise and fall changed over time. The era of this data has many influential moments, mainly the rise of TikTok and other short-form video sharing platforms, like Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts 10. This coincided with the COVID-19 pandemic, which forced everyone inside and made social media one of the main forms of human connection.
